title: Every DGFT service is set to go online by 31 March 2027, so exporters can skip office trips
subtitle: Piyush Goyal set the deadline while opening the commerce ministry's first one-roof offices in Jaipur, with old records to be scanned too.
content_html:
Picture a young trader in Jaipur who wants to send handmade quilts to a buyer in Europe. Until now, some of the paperwork for that could mean a trip to a government office. On Wednesday, 4 November 2026, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal set 31 March 2027 as the deadline to put every service of the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) online. The goal: from 1 April 2027, nobody should have to walk into a DGFT office for these services.

He made the announcement while opening two new offices in Jaipur, called Vanijya Bhawan and Udyog Bhawan, over a video link. Here is what the plan says, what DGFT does, and how this could change things for anyone who wants to start an export business.

First, what is DGFT?

Think of DGFT as the umpire of India's foreign trade. It is the agency of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry that runs the rules for buying from and selling to other countries. Its local offices are called Regional Authorities, and its head office sits in Udyog Bhavan in New Delhi.

For most new traders, the first meeting with DGFT is the Importer Exporter Code, or IEC. This is a business ID number, a bit like a player's registration number before a cricket match. According to DGFT's own page on the IEC, no goods can be exported from India or imported into India without one, unless the rules give a specific exemption. Since GST came in, the IEC number is the same as the firm's PAN, but DGFT still issues it on an application. To apply, a firm needs a PAN, a bank account in the firm's name and a valid address, and DGFT may check that address in person.

DGFT also handles applications for licences, permits and special approvals for some goods.

What exactly did Goyal order?

According to the ministry's press release, carried in full by Technology For You, the minister gave these directions:

  • Everything online. All processes, including applications for licences and permits, SCOMET approvals and other services, should move entirely online.
  • Old files too. Past data and records kept at DGFT's Regional Authorities around the country should be digitised, which means scanned and stored on computers, by the same date.
  • No trips after 1 April 2027. From that day, no person should be required or expected to visit these offices in person for these services.
  • A small desk for originals. Where an original paper must be seen by an officer, a small counter can be set up, and computers can be placed at office entrances so papers are checked and uploaded on the spot.
  • More trust. He encouraged self-certification, which means the business itself declares that the details are true instead of getting an officer to sign every line.
  • Simpler forms. He also called for simpler processes, formats and forms.

SCOMET is short for Special Chemicals, Organisms, Materials, Equipment and Technologies. As the name suggests, these are special kinds of goods, and shipping them out needs a separate approval from DGFT.

What could this change for a small exporter?

For a first-time seller who handles the paperwork alone, an office trip is not just bus fare. It is a day away from making, packing and selling.

Here is the before and after, in the plan's own terms. Before: some DGFT work could still need a visit to a DGFT office. After the deadline: the application goes in online, old records are already on a computer, and if an original paper must be checked, it is done at a small counter near the entrance.

Self-certification matters too. It works like a school that trusts students to mark their own attendance and only checks now and then. Fewer signatures can mean fewer days spent waiting for one.

Why open new offices if everything goes online?

This is the part that sounds odd at first. Goyal opened Vanijya Bhawan and Udyog Bhawan in Jaipur, and with that, Rajasthan became the first state to bring the offices of the Commerce and Industry Ministry and the bodies linked to it together at one place.

The idea is a one-stop shop, like a food court where you get chai, dosa and juice at one table instead of walking to three stalls. The minister said the ministry has around 500 offices and 46 organisations. Most of these offices will slowly move into shared buildings like the Jaipur one. Some large campuses, such as the ECGC office in Mumbai, will keep running on their own.

These shared centres will not only serve the offices sitting inside them. They will help people with services from all 46 organisations. If an officer from one organisation is not there, visitors can talk to that officer over a video call. Goyal directed that every shared office should have proper video call setups, with two or three counters in bigger centres. He wants the same model in every state capital.

Why the hurry?

The minister linked the plan to India's new trade deals and new markets, which mean more work for his ministry. The GG News report on the Jaipur event says he spoke of India's goal of becoming a USD 30 trillion economy by 2047. The press release adds that he called time "of the essence" because global trade is uncertain right now, and that the ability to compete is crucial for success. The same report also notes his call for deemed approvals, which means a request counts as approved if the office does not reply in time, wherever that is possible.

He also asked every office to have CCTV cameras linked to a central server in Vanijya Bhawan, New Delhi, for checks at random, and said that serving citizens is the ministry's first duty.

Watch: DGFT's online system and the ministry's home

This short video from DGFT's own channel shows how a trader applies for a registration on DGFT's online platform today, the kind of service the deadline wants to make fully paperless.

This one shows Vanijya Bhawan in New Delhi, the commerce ministry's newer premises. The new Jaipur centre shares its name.

What to keep an eye on

Right now this is a deadline and a set of directions, not a finished system. The real test comes on 1 April 2027: can a first-time seller in a small town get a licence or permit done from a laptop, without ever standing in a DGFT queue? The ministry's own words set that bar: no person should be required or expected to visit.

For anyone planning to start an export business, the first step stays the same. Get the IEC, keep your PAN, bank details and firm details ready, and learn which goods need extra permits. The paperwork after that is set to move online by 31 March 2027.
